content: {"summary":"In March 2025 payments‑pgbouncer‑01 showed 100 % CPU, a sign of PgBouncer saturation. The saturation caused client queues, leading payments‑api to log PAYAPI‑E1042 and return 503 errors. Runbook RB‑011 provides a step‑by‑step diagnosis: check pool statistics, count clients per instance, verify PgBouncer CPU usage, identify long‑running queries holding server connections, confirm PostgreSQL capacity, remove the offending load, and finally verify the queues are cleared.","likely_cause":"PgBouncer saturation on payments‑pgbouncer‑01, likely due to uneven client distribution or long‑running transactions that filled server connections, causing high CPU and PAYAPI‑E1042 errors.","confidence":"high","claims":[{"text":"Payments‑api logs PAYAPI‑E1042 and returns 503 when PgBouncer is saturated.","evidence_ids":["RB-011#1"],"quote":"payments-api logs `PAYAPI-E1042` and returns `503`."},{"text":"Healthy pools have cl_waiting 0, maxwait 0, sv_active well under 40; saturation shows higher values.","evidence_ids":["RB-011#2"],"quote":"Expected when healthy: `cl_waiting` 0, `maxwait` 0, `sv_active` well under 40"},{"text":"Each instance should have roughly 80 clients, far below max_client_conn 500.","evidence_ids":["RB-011#3"],"quote":"Expected: roughly 80 on each, never near `max_client_conn` (500)."},{"text":"PgBouncer CPU should be well below 100 % of a core; 100 % indicates a bottleneck.","evidence_ids":["RB-011#4"],"quote":"Expected: well below 100% CPU."},{"text":"Normal traffic shows short statements with avg_xact_s well under 0.1; higher values point to problematic queries.","evidence_ids":["RB-011#4"],"quote":"Expected in normal traffic: short statements, `avg_xact_s` well under 0.1."},{"text":"PostgreSQL should have about 100 client backends or less, well under max_connections 200.","evidence_ids":["RB-011#5"],"quote":"Expected: about 100 (both bouncers fully open) or less, against `max_connections = 200`."}]}
